entries: As they step into the same rivers, other and still other waters flow upon them.
Heraclitus, Fragments, B12 in Diels and Kranz, fragment L in Kahn (trans. Charles H. Kahn, 1979)
Philosophy
The art of losing isn’t hard to master; / so many things seem filled with the intent / to be lost that their loss is no disaster.
Elizabeth Bishop, One Art, lines 1 to 3, Geography III (Farrar, Straus and Giroux, 1976)
Poetry
As autumn advances, the Tsuchimikado mansion looks unutterably beautiful.
Murasaki Shikibu, The Diary of Lady Murasaki, the opening sentence (trans. Richard Bowring, 1996)
Diary
There is always something left to love.
Lorraine Hansberry, A Raisin in the Sun, Act III (Lena Younger, Mama) (Random House, 1959)
Drama
It is possible that some word of me may have come to you, though even this is doubtful, since an insignificant and obscure name will scarcely penetrate far in either time or space.
Petrarch, Letter to Posterity, the opening sentence, p. 59 (trans. James Harvey Robinson, 1898)
Correspondence
Whatever we had missed, we possessed together the precious, the incommunicable past.
Willa Cather, My Ántonia, Book V, Cuzak’s Boys, chapter III, the closing sentence (Jim Burden) (1918)
Fiction
All things are changing; nothing dies.
Ovid, Metamorphoses, Book XV, line 165 (Pythagoras) (trans. Frank Justus Miller, Loeb Classical Library, 1916)
Poetry
I meant to write about death, only life came breaking in as usual.
Virginia Woolf, The Diary of Virginia Woolf, Volume Two: 1920 to 1924, the entry for 17 February 1922 (ed. Anne Olivier Bell, 1978)
Diary

Corrected the work. The sentence is not in A Writer’s Diary: a search of that 1953 selection finds it nowhere, and the entry Leonard Woolf printed for the day carries the review of Monday or Tuesday instead. It stands in the complete diary, volume two, under 17 February 1922.
What then is time? If no one asks me, I know: if I wish to explain it to one that asketh, I know not.
Augustine of Hippo, Confessions, Book XI, chapter 14 (trans. E. B. Pusey, 1838)
Philosophy
All photographs are memento mori. To take a photograph is to participate in another person’s (or thing’s) mortality, vulnerability, mutability.
Susan Sontag, On Photography, In Plato’s Cave (Farrar, Straus and Giroux, 1977)
Essay
But where are the snows of yester-year?
François Villon, The Ballad of Dead Ladies, the refrain, line 8 (trans. Dante Gabriel Rossetti, 1870)
Poetry

Corrected the citation. Page 237 belongs to the Complete Poetical Works of 1887, not to the Poems of 1870 where the translation stands at pages 176 to 177, so the refrain is now located by line in Rossetti’s translation of 1870. The wording of the refrain is unchanged.
I didn’t go to the moon, I went much further—for time is the longest distance between two places.
Tennessee Williams, The Glass Menagerie, scene seven (Tom Wingfield) (Random House, 1945)
Drama

The publisher was corrected. The Glass Menagerie was first published by Random House in 1945, and New Directions reprinted it in 1949, so no New Directions edition of 1945 exists. The wording of the closing speech is unchanged.
God knows I never sought anything in you except yourself; I wanted simply you, nothing of yours.
Heloise, The Letters of Abelard and Heloise, The Personal Letters, Letter 1 (trans. Betty Radice, 1974)
Correspondence

Corrected the locator. In Betty Radice’s Penguin of 1974 the numbered sequence begins with Heloise’s first letter as Letter 1, and Letter 2 is Abelard’s reply. The Latin numbering, where her first letter is Epistola II, caused the error. The unconfirmed page reference is dropped. Wording confirmed in a Penguin printing of Radice.
Time is the substance I am made of. Time is a river which sweeps me along, but I am the river; it is a tiger which destroys me, but I am the tiger; it is a fire which consumes me, but I am the fire.
Jorge Luis Borges, Labyrinths, A New Refutation of Time, the closing paragraph (trans. James E. Irby, 1962)
Essay

The wording is not Ruth L. C. Simms’s. Her 1964 Other Inquisitions reads that carries me away and that mangles me at page 187. This sentence is the Labyrinths English of 1962, so the work, translator and year are corrected to match the words actually printed.
The flowers withered, / Their color faded away, / While meaninglessly / I spent my days in the world / And the long rains were falling.
Ono no Komachi, Kokinshu, poem 113, in Anthology of Japanese Literature (trans. Donald Keene, 1955)
Poetry
The remedy for unpredictability, for the chaotic uncertainty of the future, is contained in the faculty to make and keep promises.
Hannah Arendt, The Human Condition, chapter V, section 33 (University of Chicago Press, 1958)
Philosophy
The flow of the river is ceaseless and its water is never the same.
Kamo no Chōmei, An Account of My Hut, the opening sentence, Anthology of Japanese Literature (trans. Donald Keene, 1955)
Essay
Imitate the trees. Learn to lose in order to recover, and remember that nothing stays the same for long, not even pain, psychic pain.
May Sarton, Journal of a Solitude, the entry for October 6th (W. W. Norton, 1973)
Diary

Corrected the citation. The wording and the entry are right, so only the page reference is changed: p. 34 could not be confirmed against the 1973 Norton text, and the dated entry locates the passage on its own.
Loveliest of what I leave behind is the sunlight, / and loveliest after that the shining stars, and the moon’s face, / but also cucumbers that are ripe, and pears, and apples.
Praxilla, Hymn to Adonis, fragment 747 PMG (Adonis) (trans. Richmond Lattimore, Greek Lyrics, 1960)
Poetry

Corrected the wording to Lattimore’s published rendering: he writes what I leave behind, not what I have left behind, and keeps lower case at the second and third line heads. No page of Greek Lyrics was sighted, so the wording rests on three independent citations of that translation.
Let us do something, while we have the chance!
Samuel Beckett, Waiting for Godot, Act II (Vladimir) (trans. the author, Grove Press, 1954)
Drama

The page range could not be confirmed against the 1954 Grove printing, so the citation stands at Act II, where Vladimir says the line while Pozzo is calling for help. The English is Beckett’s own translation of his French text of 1952.
No entertainment is so cheap as reading, nor any pleasure so lasting.
Lady Mary Wortley Montagu, letter to the Countess of Bute, 28 January 1753, The Letters and Works, vol. 2, p. 236 (ed. W. Moy Thomas, 1898)
Correspondence

The date is corrected. The sentence stands in the letter to the Countess of Bute written from Lovere on 28 January 1753, about the education of her granddaughter. The quotation books date it 30 May 1756 and cite Halsband, which could not be opened. Two printed editions carry the 1753 date.
But that was the best time of my life, and only now that it has gone from me forever—only now do I realize it.
Natalia Ginzburg, The Little Virtues, Winter in the Abruzzi, the closing sentence (trans. Dick Davis, 1985, Arcade text of 2017)
Essay

Corrected the printing. The wording quoted is the Arcade text of 2017, which sets forever as one word and realize with a z. Dick Davis’s translation was first published by Carcanet in 1985 and that printing was not opened, so the source names both.
Firewood becomes ash, and it does not become firewood again. Yet, do not suppose that the ash is after and the firewood before.
Dōgen, Shōbōgenzō, Genjōkōan, section 6, Enlightenment Unfolds, pp. 35 to 39 (trans. Robert Aitken and Kazuaki Tanahashi, 1999)
Philosophy

Two corrections. The translation is by Robert Aitken and Kazuaki Tanahashi together, not Tanahashi alone, and section 6 of Enlightenment Unfolds is added. Dōgen’s own next sentence is restored to the quotation, because the first sentence alone asserts the one way passage he immediately tells the reader not to suppose.
Pause you who read this, and think for a moment of the long chain of iron or gold, of thorns or flowers, that would never have bound you, but for the formation of the first link on one memorable day.
Charles Dickens, Great Expectations, chapter 9, the closing sentence (Pip) (1861)
Fiction
Nothing beside remains. Round the decay / Of that colossal wreck, boundless and bare / The lone and level sands stretch far away.
Percy Bysshe Shelley, ‘Ozymandias’, lines 12 to 14, Rosalind and Helen, A Modern Eclogue; with Other Poems (C. and J. Ollier, 1819), p. 92
Poetry

The proposal cited the first printing in The Examiner of 11 January 1818. That printing reads No thing beside remains and Colossal Wreck, with a comma after bare. The wording quoted here is that of the collected volume of 1819, page 92, so the citation names that book.
Switzerland is a country where very few things begin, but many things end.
F. Scott Fitzgerald, The Notebooks of F. Scott Fitzgerald, section E, Epigrams, Wise Cracks and Jokes, entry 335 (ed. Bruccoli, 1978)
Diary
See how deepest purple, brightest scarlet / open their beauty only to dry well crumbling.
Tang Xianzu, The Peony Pavilion, scene 10, The Interrupted Dream, p. 44 (Bridal Du) (trans. Cyril Birch, 2nd ed. 2002)
Drama
I am certain of nothing but of the holiness of the Heart’s affections, and the truth of Imagination.
John Keats, letter to Benjamin Bailey, 22 November 1817, Letters of John Keats to His Family and Friends, p. 41 (ed. Sidney Colvin, 1891)
Correspondence

The citation now names the edition whose wording this is: Sidney Colvin’s 1891 Letters of John Keats to His Family and Friends, p. 41, which prints a comma after affections. The Rollins text of 1958 could not be opened, and reference books citing it give a shorter reading without the second of.
A free man thinks of death least of all things; and his wisdom is a meditation not of death but of life.
Baruch Spinoza, Ethics, Part IV, Proposition 67 (trans. R. H. M. Elwes, 1883)
Philosophy
If we want things to stay as they are, things will have to change.
Giuseppe Tomasi di Lampedusa, The Leopard, chapter 1 (Tancredi Falconeri) (trans. Archibald Colquhoun, 1960)
Fiction

The locator is corrected. Colquhoun’s English text is divided into chapters, not parts, and Tancredi says this in chapter 1, Introduction to the Prince. The page and imprint proposed, Harvill 1996 p. 19, could not be confirmed: printings differ, one giving p. 19 and another p. 29, so the page is dropped.
Do any human beings ever realize life while they live it?—every, every minute?
Thornton Wilder, Our Town, Act III (Emily Webb) (Coward-McCann, 1938)
Drama

unused.quote: A classic is a book that has never finished saying what it has to say.
unused.source: Italo Calvino, Why Read the Classics?, definition 6, The New York Review of Books, 9 October 1986 (trans. Patrick Creagh)

unused.quote: Listen to this reed how it complains: it is telling a tale of separations.
unused.source: Rumi, The Masnavi, Book I, line 1, the opening line (trans. Reynold A. Nicholson, 1926)

unused.quote: I have finished a monument more lasting than bronze and loftier than the Pyramids’ royal pile, one that no wasting rain, no furious north wind can destroy, or the countless chain of years and the ages’ flight.
unused.source: Horace, Odes, Book III, ode 30, lines 1 to 5 (trans. C. E. Bennett, 1914)

unused.quote: As firmly cemented clam shells / Fall apart in autumn, / So I must take to the road again, / Farewell, my friends.
unused.source: Matsuo Bashō, The Narrow Road to the Deep North, the closing verse at Ogaki (trans. Nobuyuki Yuasa, 1966)

unused.quote: I had a farm in Africa, at the foot of the Ngong Hills.
unused.source: Isak Dinesen, Out of Africa, Book One, The Ngong Farm, the opening sentence (Putnam, 1937)

unused.quote: In spite of illness, in spite even of the arch-enemy sorrow, one can remain alive long past the usual date of disintegration if one is unafraid of change, insatiable in intellectual curiosity, interested in big things, and happy in small ways.
unused.source: Edith Wharton, A Backward Glance, A First Word, third paragraph (D. Appleton-Century, 1934)

unused.quote: Wherefore he resolved to have a moving image of eternity, and when he set in order the heaven, he made this image eternal but moving according to number, while eternity itself rests in unity; and this image we call time.
unused.source: Plato, Timaeus, 37d (Timaeus) (trans. Benjamin Jowett, 1892)
unused.note: The cosmology at 37d is spoken by Timaeus of Locri, not by Plato in his own voice, so the speaker is named after the locator, as the year’s other Plato lines do. The Jowett wording is unchanged and was checked against the 1892 text.

unused.quote: Some races wax and others wane, and in a short space the tribes of living things are changed, and like runners hand on the torch of life.
unused.source: Lucretius, De Rerum Natura, Book II, lines 77 to 79 (trans. Cyril Bailey, 1910)

unused.quote: Life is a pure flame, and we live by an invisible Sun within us.
unused.source: Thomas Browne, Hydriotaphia, Urn-Burial, chapter V (1658)

unused.quote: If by eternity is understood not endless temporal duration but timelessness, then he lives eternally who lives in the present.
unused.source: Ludwig Wittgenstein, Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus, proposition 6.4311 (trans. C. K. Ogden, 1922)

unused.quote: Duration is the continuous progress of the past which gnaws into the future and which swells as it advances.
unused.source: Henri Bergson, Creative Evolution, chapter I (trans. Arthur Mitchell, 1911)

unused.quote: Life is not a series of gig lamps symmetrically arranged; life is a luminous halo, a semi-transparent envelope surrounding us from the beginning of consciousness to the end.
unused.source: Virginia Woolf, Modern Fiction, The Common Reader (Hogarth Press, 1925)
unused.note: Corrected the wording. The Common Reader of 1925 reads life is a luminous halo. The reading but a luminous halo belongs to the earlier version of the essay, Modern Novels, printed in the Times Literary Supplement in 1919.

unused.quote: Attachment is a manufacturer of illusions and whoever wants reality ought to be detached.
unused.source: Simone Weil, Gravity and Grace, Detachment, p. 59 (trans. Arthur Wills, 1952)
unused.note: Corrected the locator. The sentence stands in the chapter Detachment on page 59 of the Wills translation, published by Putnam in New York in 1952, not on page 13. The wording is verbatim in that text.

unused.quote: For nothing is fixed, forever and forever and forever, it is not fixed; the earth is always shifting, the light is always changing, the sea does not cease to grind down rock.
unused.source: James Baldwin, Nothing Personal, the closing passage (Atheneum, 1964)

unused.quote: The answer must be, I think, that beauty and grace are performed whether or not we will or sense them. The least we can do is try to be there.
unused.source: Annie Dillard, Pilgrim at Tinker Creek, chapter 1, Heaven and Earth in Jest (Harper’s Magazine Press, 1974)

unused.quote: I think we are well advised to keep on nodding terms with the people we used to be, whether we find them attractive company or not.
unused.source: Joan Didion, Slouching Towards Bethlehem, On Keeping a Notebook (Farrar, Straus and Giroux, 1968)

unused.quote: Better by far you should forget and smile / Than that you should remember and be sad.
unused.source: Christina Rossetti, ‘Remember’, lines 13 to 14, Goblin Market and Other Poems (Macmillan, 1862)

unused.quote: Though a country be sundered, hills and rivers endure; / And spring comes green again to trees and grasses / Where petals have been shed like tears / And lonely birds have sung their grief.
unused.source: Du Fu, A Spring View, lines 1 to 4, The Jade Mountain, p. 148 (trans. Witter Bynner with Kiang Kang-hu, 1929)

unused.quote: Though leaves are many, the root is one; / Through all the lying days of my youth / I swayed my leaves and flowers in the sun; / Now I may wither into the truth.
unused.source: W. B. Yeats, The Coming of Wisdom with Time, the whole poem, The Green Helmet and Other Poems (Cuala Press, 1910)

unused.quote: We look at the world once, in childhood. / The rest is memory.
unused.source: Louise Glück, Nostos, the closing lines, Meadowlands (Ecco Press, 1996)

unused.quote: But not because of its magnificence / Dear is the Casuarina to my soul: / Beneath it we have played; though years may roll, / O sweet companions, loved with love intense, / For your sakes, shall the tree be ever dear.
unused.source: Toru Dutt, Our Casuarina Tree, stanza 3, lines 1 to 5, Ancient Ballads and Legends of Hindustan (Kegan Paul, Trench and Co., 1882)
unused.note: Corrected the locator. Each stanza of the poem runs to eleven lines and the quotation is only the first five of stanza three, so the locator now names those lines. The wording stands as printed, with the colon after soul and the comma after sakes.

unused.quote: Barrabás came to us by sea, the child Clara wrote in her delicate calligraphy.
unused.source: Isabel Allende, The House of the Spirits, chapter 1, the opening sentence (trans. Magda Bogin, 1985)
unused.note: Verified opening line in Bogin’s translation; it returns as the novel’s last line. Held for a month that can use a pure opening.

unused.quote: Eternity is in love with the productions of time.
unused.source: William Blake, The Marriage of Heaven and Hell, Proverbs of Hell, plate 7 (c. 1790 to 1793)
unused.note: Verified, the tenth Proverb of Hell, plate 7. Time and what is made in it: an impermanence line more than a discipline line.

unused.quote: Our life is March weather, savage and serene in one hour.
unused.source: Ralph Waldo Emerson, Representative Men, IV, Montaigne; or, the Skeptic (Phillips, Sampson and Company, 1850), p. 174
unused.note: Verified in the 1850 first edition, p. 174. It is about the inconstancy of moods, which is impermanence rather than renewal, and the March refuter named it the first to drop.

unused.quote: The butterfly counts not months but moments, / and has time enough.
unused.source: Rabindranath Tagore, Fireflies, p. 15 (Macmillan, New York, 1928)
unused.note: Corrected in re-verification to a page locator. Held: a two line poem about moments, for the month of passing things.

unused.quote: My candle burns at both ends; / It will not last the night; / But ah, my foes, and oh, my friends— / It gives a lovely light!
unused.source: Edna St. Vincent Millay, First Fig, the whole poem, A Few Figs from Thistles (Harper and Brothers, 1922)
unused.note: Corrected the edition to the Harper text of 1922. Held: a candle that will not last the night is impermanence.

unused.quote: He could see plainly that she was not herself. That is, he could not see that she was becoming herself and daily casting aside that fictitious self which we assume like a garment with which to appear before the world.
unused.source: Kate Chopin, The Awakening, chapter XIX (1899)
unused.note: Verified in chapter XIX of 1899. Casting aside the fictitious self, which is a truth line held for want of a day.

unused.quote: The public must decide whether it wishes to continue on the present road, and it can do so only when in full possession of the facts.
unused.source: Rachel Carson, Silent Spring, chapter 2, The Obligation to Endure (Houghton Mifflin, 1962)
unused.note: Verified in chapter 2 of Silent Spring. Full possession of the facts, a public truth line.

unused.quote: I’m nobody! Who are you? / Are you nobody, too?
unused.source: Emily Dickinson, ‘I’m nobody! Who are you?’, Poems, Second Series, Life I, lines 1 to 2 (Roberts Brothers, 1891)
unused.note: Verified in Poems, Second Series of 1891. Two lines only, in that edition’s lineation.

unused.quote: Some men say an army of horse and some men say an army on foot and some men say an army of ships is the most beautiful thing on the black earth. But I say it is what you love.
unused.source: Sappho, If Not, Winter, Fragment 16, lines 1 to 4 (trans. Anne Carson, 2002)
unused.note: Carried from January, verified in Carson, p. 27. Before it lands, the four lines must be marked with slashes in Carson’s lineation, which nobody has yet checked against the page; it is carried as prose.

unused.quote: Beauty is no quality in things themselves: It exists merely in the mind which contemplates them; and each mind perceives a different beauty.
unused.source: David Hume, Essays, Moral, Political, and Literary, Of the Standard of Taste (ed. Miller, pp. 229 to 230)
unused.note: Corrected in re-verification. Held: Hume sets the sentence out as the sceptical case and the next paragraph restrains it, so it wants a month about seeing clearly.

unused.quote: The most exhausting thing in life, I have discovered, is being insincere.
unused.source: Anne Morrow Lindbergh, Gift from the Sea, chapter 2, Channelled Whelk (1955)
unused.note: Hedged: Gift from the Sea was never opened and the reference readings agree on chapter 2. Held for a month about sincerity.

unused.quote: I did not care what it was all about. All I wanted to know was how to live in it. Maybe if you found out how to live in it you learned from that what it was all about.
unused.source: Ernest Hemingway, The Sun Also Rises, Book II, chapter 14 (Jake Barnes) (Charles Scribner’s Sons, 1926)
unused.note: Verified in the Scribner text of 1926. Held: Jake wants to know how to live in it, which is a search for clarity.

unused.quote: Against the assault of laughter nothing can stand.
unused.source: Mark Twain, The Mysterious Stranger, ch. 10 (Satan) (Harper and Brothers, 1916)
unused.note: Verified. Held: laughter is the weapon here, not endurance, so it wants the lighter month.

unused.quote: Music was my refuge. I could crawl into the spaces between the notes and curl my back to loneliness.
unused.source: Maya Angelou, Singin’ and Swingin’ and Gettin’ Merry Like Christmas, chapter 1, the opening sentences (Random House, 1976)
unused.note: Verified. Held: Maya Angelou stands in July with Still I Rise, and one person may stand once a month.

unused.quote: But he that dares not grasp the thorn / Should never crave the rose.
unused.source: Anne Brontë, The Narrow Way (1848), lines 15 to 16, in The Complete Poems of Anne Brontë (ed. Clement Shorter, 1920), p. 145
unused.note: Verified in Shorter’s 1920 Complete Poems, p. 145: he that, not he who. Add the page to the source. Held to keep March under the cap for lines originally in English.

unused.quote: I will mount a long wind some day and break the heavy waves / And set my cloudy sail straight and bridge the deep, deep sea.
unused.source: Li Bai, The Hard Road, closing couplet, The Jade Mountain, p. 70 (trans. Witter Bynner, 1929)
unused.note: Verified. One Bynner poem landed already and only one may stand in a month, and the hard road is a courage line.

unused.quote: The wide world is all about you: you can fence yourselves in, but you cannot for ever fence it out.
unused.source: J. R. R. Tolkien, The Fellowship of the Ring, Book I, chapter 3, Three is Company (George Allen and Unwin, 1954) (Gildor Inglorion)
unused.note: Verified with the two-word for ever. Tolkien’s small hands is already held for September, so this goes to July.

unused.quote: That’s no way to treat adventures. Never say ‘no’ to adventures. Always say ‘yes’, otherwise you’ll lead a very dull life.
unused.source: Ian Fleming, Chitty-Chitty-Bang-Bang: The Magical Car, Adventure Number Two (Commander Caractacus Pott) (Jonathan Cape, 1964)
unused.note: Verified. Held: Commander Pott’s counsel is about saying yes to danger, which suits a month of trial.

unused.quote: My way of joking is to tell the truth. It’s the funniest joke in the world.
unused.source: Bernard Shaw, John Bull’s Other Island, Act II, his reply to Nora Reilly (Peter Keegan)
unused.note: Verified as Peter Keegan’s reply to Nora Reilly. Held because the drama lane was already full.

unused.quote: I am large, I contain multitudes.
unused.source: Walt Whitman, Leaves of Grass, ‘Song of Myself’, section 51, 1881 text
unused.note: Verified; parenthetical in the source. Not a beginning line so much as a truth-and-clarity line.

unused.quote: Travel is in my opinion a very profitable exercise; the soul is there continually employed in observing new and unknown things, and I do not know, as I have often said a better school wherein to model life than by incessantly exposing to it the diversity of so many other lives, fancies, and usances, and by making it relish a perpetual variety of forms of human nature.
unused.source: Michel de Montaigne, Essays, Book III, ch. 9, Of Vanity (trans. Charles Cotton, revised by W. Carew Hazlitt, 1877)
unused.note: Verified. Another Montaigne is already held for May, so this goes on to the month of clear seeing.

unused.quote: There is no foreign land; it is the traveller only that is foreign, and now and again, by a flash of recollection, lights up the contrasts of the earth.
unused.source: Robert Louis Stevenson, The Silverado Squatters, Part II, With the Children of Israel, chapter III, The Return (Chatto and Windus, 1883)
unused.note: Corrected: the sentence is in The Return, Part II. Held: it is the traveller only that is foreign is a correction of the eye, which is June.

unused.quote: The world of dew / Is the world of dew, / And yet . . . / And yet . . .
unused.source: Kobayashi Issa, The Year of My Life, pp. 103 to 104, the elegy for his daughter (trans. Nobuyuki Yuasa, 1960)
unused.note: Held, not refused: the verse ends on the translator’s ellipsis, so it cannot carry the terminal stop every card needs. It would need a translation that closes on a stop, and nothing else about it was in doubt.

report.thinnestLane: Fiction, three survivors in the whole pool
